recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Thousands of galaxies spread across the dark backdrop of space in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field 2014, a small section of sky in the southern constellation Fornax. The image holds roughly 10,000 galaxies, and the most distant are seen as they were only a few hundred million years after the big bang.

Astronomers had already studied this field in visible and near-infrared light. The 2014 version adds ultraviolet, combining the full range of colors available to Hubble. Exposures from 2002 to 2012, made with two Hubble cameras (ACS and WFC3), went into it, using 841 orbits of observing time.

The hottest, largest and youngest stars give off ultraviolet light, so it shows which galaxies are forming stars and where. That fills a gap for the period, between about 5 billion and 10 billion light-years away, when most of the universe's stars were born. Because Earth's atmosphere blocks most ultraviolet light, the work needs a telescope in space.

understand.summary: A composite of 13 filters from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras, spanning ultraviolet to near-infrared. NASA shows the ultraviolet and blue-visible filters (F150LP, F225W, F275W, F336W, F435W and F606W) in blue, F775W, F814W, F850LP and F105W in green, and F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: The exposures add up to about 600 hours and include ultraviolet and infrared light that the eye cannot see, revealing galaxies far beyond its reach.

explore: Researchers describe the study behind it, called Ultraviolet Coverage of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, as the missing link in star formation. Principal investigator Harry Teplitz of Caltech compared the earlier gap to studying family histories without knowing about the grade-school children. The ultraviolet data were expected to be combined with infrared data from the James Webb Space Telescope.
